title: Redwood discovery - reliability & multi-region fallbacks with Praxis Systems
topics: hosted vs dedicated vs private deployment
security: SOC2, KMS, audit logs, SSO
summary: Discovery call to capture Praxis Systems' requirements for reliability and incident tolerance across Redwood Hosted/Dedicated/Private options. Key concerns: multi-region failover latency, deterministic SLA targets, data residency/KMS, and proving behavior in POC. Agreed next steps: send security pack, pricing for Dedicated (committed nodes) and Hosted fallback configs, schedule pilot benchmarking week.
action_items: Arielle Kim - Send security whitepaper + SOC2 report - due 2027-11-18
Devon Park - Share suggested Dedicated sizing and latency/cost estimate spreadsheet - due 2027-11-19
Maya Patel - Share Praxis traffic profile and peak TPS numbers - due 2027-11-17
next_steps: Redwood to email SOC2 + security pack
Schedule 1-week POC (benchmarks) w/ dedicated nodes and multi-region failover
Pricing sheet for Dedicated commit + Hosted fallback plan
Set up follow-up technical deep-dive with Praxis SREs
transcript:
Meeting header:
Date: 2027-11-14
Start: 16:00 UTC
Duration: ~45 minutes
Attendees: Arielle Kim (Redwood AE), Devon Park (Redwood SE), Liam O'Connor (CTO - Praxis), Maya Patel (SRE - Praxis), Jordan Reyes (Product - Praxis)

Summary: quick intro, then go through availability, multi-region failover expectations, security constraints, and POC scope.

[00:00] Arielle: Hey everyone, thanks for joining, um, we're excited to chat through reliability and incident tolerance for the Praxis use case. I think Devon will cover the technical bits.
[00:12] Devon: Hi all. Quick agenda - hosted vs dedicated vs private tradeoffs, fallback policies, multi-region routing and SLAs, and then we can sketch a POC for benchmarking.
[00:25] Liam: Sounds good. For context, our main product uses LLMs for realtime recommendations and chat assistance. Peak is about 220 reqs/s during the morning spike,  p95 latency targets for user-facing flows are under 200ms. We're particularly worried about regional outages - we have users across EU and NA.
[00:43] Maya: Also, security is huge: must be SOC2 compliant, keys in our KMS, audit logs, and SSO with SAML. We can't ship customer PII outside EU without residency guarantees.
[01:05] Arielle: Totally. On the residency side we support region pinning for private and Dedicated, and Hosted has region routing options - we'll share the exact certs and docs.
[01:18] Devon: To frame the options briefly: Hosted is fastest to integrate, supports multi-region routing with automated failover but has shared capacity; Dedicated gives you reserved GPU pools in a region with predictable throughput and isolation; Private (VPC/on-prem) gives you full control for residency and KMS.
[01:40] Jordan: If we go Dedicated, can we still get cross-region failover? We want to send traffic to EU primary but fail to NA if EU is down.
[01:52] Devon: Yes - Dedicated supports cross-region replica pools or can use Hosted as a fallback. Typical patterns: 1) Active-primary EU Dedicated with NA Dedicated or Hosted fallback; 2) Active-active across EU/NA with stateful KV cache replication. The tradeoff is cost and replication complexity.
[02:18] Liam: Replicating KV cache worries me - state consistency during failover. How does Redwood handle KV/prefix cache to avoid cold-starts?
[02:29] Devon: Good question. We have prefix/KV cache mechanisms - for Dedicated we can replicate KV snapshots asynchronously to the standby region; during failover the standby warms the KV. It isn't perfectly synchronous so you might see some increased latency or partial cache misses for a short window. For ultra-low RTO we recommend an active-active config with key migration and consistent hashing, though that adds operational overhead.
[02:59] Maya: What's the expected RTO for a region outage with the fallback to Hosted? Say EU Dedicated primary, fallback to Hosted NA.
[03:10] Devon: In our experience, automated routing failover to a compatible model variant in another region is typically sub-90s to start returning responses, but full warm state can take longer - think 2-5 minutes for caches to warm; that depends on your session lengths and KV footprint. We also do graceful degradation: shorter contexts, lower token budgets and model-variant fallbacks reduce cost/latency.
[03:42] Liam: 90 seconds is okay as long as user-visible errors are low. Can SLA reflect that? What SLA numbers do you offer for Dedicated?
[03:54] Arielle: Our Dedicated offering comes with an SLA - currently we target 99.9% for regional availability at the cluster level for committed capacity. For higher tiers we can discuss 99.95 with multi-AZ multi-region configurations. SLA details depend on committed nodes and topology. We'll send the SLA doc.
[04:15] Jordan: During failover, do requests get queued? Or do we see immediate 5xx errors?
[04:22] Devon: There are configurable fallback policies. By default, Redwood attempts retry/backoff and then route to a fallback model/region if configured. You can choose fail-open (serve best-effort) or fail-closed (return error). We typically recommend a fail-open policy with a lightweight model variant for user-facing features.
[04:43] Maya: And about consistency - are audit logs preserved across failover? We need a single view for compliance.
[04:51] Devon: Audit logs are centralized to the control plane or to your SIEM depending on deployment. For Dedicated and Private you can forward logs to your audit stack (CloudWatch/BigQuery/Splunk). During failover log ingestion continues; it's just written from the active region. We include metadata for failover events so you can trace which region served each request.
[05:12] Liam: KMS - can we use our AWS KMS or an HSM?
[05:17] Arielle: Yes, for Private and Dedicated we support customer-managed KMS keys (AWS KMS, Azure Key Vault, or HSM via integration). Hosted supports envelope encryption with customer keys via bring-your-own-key options for enterprise.
[05:32] Jordan: Ok, POC scope - we'd want Redwood to demonstrate: 1) failover from EU to NA while maintaining p95 under 800ms for degraded mode; 2) a Dedicated sizing that meets 220 reqs/s with 200ms p95 in normal mode; 3) security checklist satisfied.
[05:54] Devon: That's reasonable. For the Dedicated sizing I'd propose a 4-GPU pool (NVIDIA A100 equivalent) as a starting point, then we can run concurrency benchmarks. We'll provide a suggested autoscale and burst config.
[06:10] Maya: For the benchmarks, we need to know how you measure latency (end-to-end vs inference-only) and whether streaming is supported.
[06:19] Devon: We'll provide both numbers. E2E includes network + routing + runtime; inference-only is kernel execution. Streaming is supported for chat flows; p95 for streaming can be tricky to compare so we'll include token-based throughput and latency measures.
[06:36] Liam: Do you offer canary rollouts and automatic fallbacks for regression detection? We want safe deploys of model updates.
[06:45] Devon: Yes - rollouts support canary percentages, A/B, and automatic rollback if quality regression alerts trigger. We can tie regressions to prompt sets and evals you provide.
[06:57] Jordan: How about runbook automation during incidents? Can Redwood trigger webhooks or PagerDuty events?
[07:03] Arielle: We integrate with PagerDuty, Slack, and can run synthetic tests. We'll include runbook examples - many customers wire our alerts into their incident response.
[07:14] Maya: One more on cost - if we use Hosted as fallback most of the time will be in Dedicated EU; fallback to Hosted NA might increase egress and per-token cost. Want to make sure cost spikes are bounded.
[07:28] Devon: Right - we have policy controls to limit fallback usage and rate-limit on the fallback path. There's also model-tier mapping: fallback can target a cheaper quantized model variant to keep unit cost low. We'll show cost estimates in the sizing spreadsheet.
[07:48] Liam: Competitors - we've looked at OpenCloud AI and Infralabs; primary differentiator for Redwood is the unified runtime across deployment modes?
[07:57] Arielle: Exactly. We try to keep the same API and rollout semantics across Hosted, Dedicated, and Private so you can move between them without heavy code changes.
[08:08] Jordan: Ok, timeline - we'd like a POC in the next 3 weeks to present to the execs. Is that realistic?
[08:15] Arielle: Yes, we can stand up a POC in 2-3 weeks assuming we get the traffic profile and a short legal/data access form completed. We'll send the agreement template.
[08:27] Devon: For the POC I'll need a sample traffic replay or a JMeter script and a baseline prompt set for quality checks.
[08:36] Maya: We'll prepare that. Also can we get your SOC2 and a vendor security questionnaire?
[08:41] Arielle: Yes, I'll send the SOC2 report and our security pack after the call.
[08:46] Liam: Perfect. Final quick question - do you do DR drills with customers? Could we schedule a failover test during the POC?
[08:55] Devon: Absolutely; we usually run a scheduled failover exercise and measure RTO/RPO and user impact. We'll run that as part of the POC.
[09:05] Arielle: Great. Quick recap of next steps: we'll email the security docs and SLA, Devon will send sizing and a benchmark plan, Praxis will share traffic profile and agree on POC dates.
[09:18] Jordan: Thanks everyone, talk soon.
[09:22] Arielle: Thanks all. Bye.

Notes (transcription imperfect in places: "KV" appeared as "K-V" in a couple spots; Redwood product names sometimes mistranscribed).
